newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Airline chiefs meet on clouded industry outlook.
newsitem.headline: Airline chiefs meet on clouded industry outlook.

text.p: World airline executives, facing a mounting challenge to reshape operations in tune with the integration of the international economy, meet this week to discuss new directions for the booming industry.

At the annual general meeting of the global airline body, the International Air Transport Association (IATA), they are also expected to hear that collectively their companies seem headed for a record profit for the third year in a row.

But looming in the background are growing worries about the effects of rising fuel costs, a row with the United States over passenger compensation, and concern that any new conflict in the Middle East could hit their companies hard.

Industry officials say they are also well aware of an increasing perception among passengers that the new alliances many carriers have formed are aimed more at shareholder comfort than at customer satisfaction and safety.

And some say the weekend recommendation from U.S. aerospace giant Boeing Co that all 2,700 of its 737 jetliners in service be given quick tests for potential rudder system problems will also focus minds on the safety issue.
The centrepiece of the two-day meeting will be an address on Monday by IATA Director-General Pierre Jeanniot on the overall state of the industry and the problems it faces.

Jeanniot is expected to report that the now over 250 airlines belonging to the Geneva- and Montreal-based IATA, who together account for 98 per cent of all international scheduled flights, are heading for another healthy profit this year.
But there are signs that the final figure could be lower than the $6 billion the former Air Canada chief predicted in April this year -- partly because of fuel price rises.

The industry worldwide has been looking for an overall good return this year to fill the hole left in its coffers in the lean years of 1990-93 when recession and the effects of the 1990-91 Gulf conflict brought a total loss of $15,6 billion.

This year, fuel costs for world carriers -- around 11 per cent of their operational outgoings -- have climbed by around 15 per cent, from an average of U.S. 65.2 cents a gallon in 1995 to a high this autumn of U.S. 77.5 cents.

IATA, set up in 1945 by 57 airlines from 31 countries to promote easier and safer air travel and freight movement, revealed last week it had called an emergency meeting in Geneva on November 13 to consider concerted action.
But many airlines, especially in Europe, have already said they will have to start putting up prices this winter.

IATA officials say the increased costs, if current price levels are maintained, will reduce the airlines' ability to buy new-generation aircraft which burn less fuel and emit gases less likely to contribute to global warming.

Another theme of the meeting will be an effort by IATA and the Montreal-based United Nations agency, the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO), to improve settlement of claims by passengers and shippers for loss and death.

Earlier this year, key IATA members agreed on replacing liability limits set out in the 1946 Warsaw Convention -- shaped to give protection to a young industry recovering from World War Two -- with a pledge to pay full "compensatory damages."
Current limits under the Convention, which IATA officials say airlines recognise are grossly out of date, range from $75,000 in the United States to $150,000 in Europe and $350,000 in Australasia.

But IATA says the Department of Transport in the United States, the world's biggest aviation market, is effectively blocking the change -- to have gone into effect on November 1 -- and has accused it publicly of acting illegally.
